title: The first haircut
hook: at three, in many Hasidic and some Sephardi families

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pidyon haben, and your line was redemption: five coins, and a father who chose his son. Did you tell someone you'd choose them? Today, a child turns three. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

A little boy sits on his father's lap, curls down past his shoulders. He has never had a haircut. Not once. The living room is full of relatives and neighbors, and a pair of scissors is going around the room like a microphone at a wedding. One by one, each guest snips a single lock. An uncle. A grandmother. The rabbi. A cousin who is barely taller than the boy. Somebody's handing out candy. By the end the boy looks like a different child, and at the sides of his head, two locks have been left long, on purpose. Today's word is this party.
screen: `CURLS NEVER CUT.` → `THE SCISSORS GO AROUND.` → `TWO LOCKS LEFT LONG.`

segments.voice: Upsherin. A Yiddish name for a child's first haircut, held at three in many Hasidic families and, in their own versions, in some Sephardi families too. Turn it four ways. First, the tree. Leviticus says that when Israel plants a fruit tree, its fruit is not to be eaten for three years. In the fourth year it is holy, and after that it is food. And a verse in Deuteronomy, the one about fruit trees in a siege, is read by some as comparing a person to a tree of the field. Some families draw the line between the two: a child, like a young tree, is left untouched for three years, and then the first harvest. It's a custom, not a written law. Second, the side locks. Leviticus also says not to round off the corners of the head. So at the first haircut, the hair at the temples is left long. These are the peyot, the side locks, and for the boy they start on this day. Third, the first things. In some families, an upsherin is also the day a boy first wears a kippah and the fringed garment called tzitzit. Some families bring him to start learning his letters that week. The haircut is the outward sign; the inner change is that the child now begins to be taught. Fourth, the whole room. The custom doesn't give the scissors to a barber alone. Each guest takes a turn. Everyone who snips a curl has a hand in raising this child. Three years of waiting, and then a whole community leans in at once.
screen: `THREE YEARS, LIKE A YOUNG TREE.` · `THE CORNERS OF THE HEAD.` · `KIPPAH, TZITZIT, FIRST LETTERS.` · `EVERY GUEST TAKES A TURN.` · then, large: `THREE YEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark one milestone. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that has been growing quietly for a while. A child, a friendship, a skill, a garden, a recovery. Something you've been patient with. Ask: has it reached a point worth marking? Picture the people who'd have a hand in it, each taking a turn. Then choose one small way to mark it: a meal, a message, a photo, a few words said out loud. If you pray, you can give thanks for what has grown. The bell holds the time.
Upsherin. The first haircut at three: the young tree, the side locks left long, and a turn with the scissors for everyone. Today's word.
Your line: three years. Today, mark the milestone you chose, however small, and invite one other person to have a hand in it. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: In many Hasidic families, and in some Sephardi families with their own versions, a boy's hair is left uncut until he turns three; at the upsherin, guests each cut a lock, the side locks are left, and he often begins wearing a kippah and tzitzit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute first-haircut party.
what it means: three years untouched, then each guest cuts a lock, the side locks stay, and the child begins to be taught.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19's young tree, three years and then holy fruit, read with one reading of Deuteronomy 20, which compares a person to a tree.

notes: Leviticus 19:23–25 (three years forbidden, the fourth holy), 19:27 (corners of the head) and Deuteronomy 20:19 (a person compared to a tree of the field) paraphrased. The Deuteronomy reading follows the traditional Jewish interpretation; confirm.
The upsherin is described as a custom ('not a law, and those who keep it say so'); confirm this is fair to communities that keep it strictly.
Sephardi versions (sometimes called chalaka) left unnamed; confirm.
Kippah, tzitzit and beginning to learn letters described with 'in many families' / 'some families'; the honey-on-letters custom is held for the next day.
The script speaks of a boy, as the custom is mainly for boys; some families mark a girl's third birthday in other ways (e.g. lighting Shabbat candles). Keeper to decide whether to add a line.
Original-language card left null: 'upsherin' is Yiddish and the Hebrew/Ladino names vary.
